questions.q: Which organelle is the site of protein synthesis?
questions.why: Ribosomes translate mRNA into polypeptides.

questions.q: Which feature is found in prokaryotic cells?
questions.why: Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles; their ribosomes are 70S.

questions.q: The resolution of a light microscope is limited by…
questions.why: Resolution is about half the wavelength used; electrons have much shorter wavelengths.

questions.q: An eyepiece graticule must be calibrated using…
questions.why: The stage micrometer's known divisions give the value of each graticule unit at that magnification.

long.q: In an electron micrograph a mitochondrion measures 18 mm. Its actual length is 3 µm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
scheme: A1: magnification = 18 000 ÷ 3 = × 6000

questions.q: Which bond joins two α-glucose molecules in maltose?
questions.why: A condensation reaction forms an α-1,4 glycosidic bond.

questions.q: What gives cellulose its strength?
o: Hydrogen bonds between parallel chains of β-glucose forming microfibrils
questions.why: Alternate β-glucose units are inverted, giving straight chains that hydrogen-bond together.

questions.q: Which level of protein structure is the sequence of amino acids?
questions.why: The primary structure determines how the chain folds.

questions.q: Why is water a good solvent?
o: It is polar, so ions and polar molecules dissolve
questions.why: Its δ+ and δ− regions surround charged and polar particles.

long.q: Describe the structure of cellulose and explain how it suits its role in plant cell walls.
scheme: B1: β-glucose monomers joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds, alternate ones rotated 180°
B1: long straight chains held together by many hydrogen bonds into microfibrils
B1: giving high tensile strength, so the wall resists bursting when the cell is turgid

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor…
o: binds to the active site, competing with the substrate
binds elsewhere and changes the active site
questions.why: Raising substrate concentration can overcome it; Vmax is unchanged.

questions.q: A low Km means the enzyme has…
questions.why: Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax; low Km means it reaches it at low concentration.

questions.q: Why are immobilised enzymes useful?
o: They work faster than free enzymes always
They can be reused and are more stable, and the product isn't contaminated
questions.why: Fixing enzymes in beads makes separation and reuse easy.

long.q: Explain how a non-competitive inhibitor affects the Vmax and the Michaelis–Menten constant (Km) of an enzyme.
scheme: B1: it binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site)
B1: changing the shape of the active site, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form
B1: Vmax is lower; adding more substrate does not overcome it
B1: Km is unchanged (the affinity of the remaining active enzymes is the same)

questions.q: In the fluid mosaic model, what makes the membrane fluid?
o: Phospholipids that move within the layer
questions.why: Phospholipids move laterally; cholesterol regulates fluidity.

questions.q: Facilitated diffusion uses…
o: channel or carrier proteins, down a concentration gradient
questions.why: It is passive, but needs proteins for polar or charged molecules.

questions.q: Water potential of pure water is…
questions.why: Ψ of pure water is 0 kPa; solutes make it negative.

long.q: A plant cell is placed in pure water. Explain, in terms of water potential, what happens to the cell.
scheme: B1: pure water has a higher (less negative) water potential than the cell (0 kPa)
B1: water moves into the cell by osmosis, down the water potential gradient, through the partially permeable membrane
B1: the cell becomes turgid; the cell wall stops it bursting

questions.q: In which stage do chromosomes line up on the equator?
questions.why: Spindle fibres attach to centromeres and align chromosomes at metaphase.

questions.q: When is DNA replicated?
questions.why: DNA synthesis happens in the S phase before mitosis.

questions.q: What is the role of telomeres?
o: Protect chromosome ends from losing genes during replication
questions.why: Repeated non-coding sequences are lost instead of genes.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative because…
o: each new molecule has one original strand and one new strand
it happens in half the cells
questions.why: Shown by the Meselson–Stahl experiment.

questions.q: Which enzyme joins Okazaki fragments?
questions.why: Ligase seals the gaps in the lagging strand.

questions.q: During translation, tRNA anticodons pair with…
questions.why: Complementary base pairing places the right amino acid.

questions.q: A substitution mutation may have no effect because…
o: the genetic code is degenerate (several codons per amino acid)
questions.why: A different codon can still code for the same amino acid.

scheme: B1: hydrogen bonds between bases break and the double helix unwinds (helicase)
B1: each strand acts as a template
B1: free nucleotides pair with complementary bases (A–T, C–G)
B1: DNA polymerase joins the nucleotides, so each new molecule has one old strand and one new strand

questions.q: What drives water up the xylem?
o: Transpiration pull, with cohesion and adhesion
questions.why: Evaporation from leaves creates tension that pulls a continuous column of water up.

questions.q: Sucrose is loaded into phloem sieve tubes by…
o: co-transport with H⁺ via companion cells
questions.why: Companion cells pump H⁺ out; sucrose re-enters with H⁺ through co-transporters.

questions.q: Xerophytes reduce water loss by…
o: sunken stomata, rolled leaves and thick cuticles
questions.why: These trap humid air and reduce the surface exposed.

questions.q: The Bohr effect means that high CO₂ concentration…
questions.why: Oxygen is released more readily where respiration is high.

questions.q: What starts each heartbeat?
questions.why: The SAN starts a wave of excitation; the AVN delays it before the ventricles contract.

questions.q: Tissue fluid forms because at the arterial end of a capillary…
o: hydrostatic pressure is greater than the osmotic pull
questions.why: Fluid is forced out; most returns at the venous end.

long.q: Explain the Bohr shift and why it is useful in actively respiring tissues.
scheme: B1: high carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen (curve shifts right)
B1: CO₂ forms carbonic acid, and H⁺ ions bind to haemoglobin forming haemoglobinic acid
B1: so more oxygen is released (unloaded) where it is needed for respiration

questions.q: What is the role of cartilage in the trachea?
questions.why: C-shaped rings stop the trachea collapsing.

questions.q: Goblet cells…
questions.why: Cilia then sweep the mucus upwards.

questions.q: Which organism causes malaria?
questions.why: Plasmodium is transmitted by female Anopheles mosquitoes.

questions.q: How does penicillin kill bacteria?
o: It stops cell wall synthesis, so cells burst
It blocks ribosomes in human cells
questions.why: Without strong walls, bacteria burst by osmosis as they grow.

long.q: Explain how a population of bacteria becomes resistant to an antibiotic.
scheme: B1: a random mutation gives a bacterium resistance (e.g. a gene for an enzyme that breaks down the antibiotic)
B1: when the antibiotic is used, resistant bacteria survive and non-resistant ones die (selection pressure)
B1: resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on the allele, also by horizontal gene transfer on plasmids

questions.q: Which cells produce antibodies?
questions.why: Activated B cells divide and differentiate into plasma cells.

questions.q: Passive immunity is…
questions.why: No memory cells are made, e.g. antibodies across the placenta.

questions.q: Monoclonal antibodies are produced by…
questions.why: They are identical and target one specific antigen.

long.q: Distinguish between active and passive immunity, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: active: the person's own immune system makes antibodies after meeting an antigen
B1: example: vaccination, or recovering from an infection
B1: passive: antibodies are given from outside; no memory cells form, so it is short-lived
B1: example: antibodies across the placenta or in breast milk, or an injection of antibodies

questions.q: Where does the Krebs cycle take place?
questions.why: Glycolysis is in the cytoplasm; link reaction and Krebs cycle in the matrix.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.why: Oxygen combines with electrons and H⁺ to form water.

questions.q: A respiratory quotient (RQ) near 0.7 suggests the substrate is…
questions.why: Carbohydrate 1.0, protein about 0.9, lipid about 0.7.

questions.q: Where does the light-dependent stage happen?
questions.why: Photosystems and the electron transport chain are in the thylakoids.

questions.q: Which enzyme fixes CO₂ in the Calvin cycle?
questions.why: Rubisco combines CO₂ with RuBP.

questions.q: A limiting factor is…
o: the factor that controls the rate because it is in shortest supply
questions.why: Increasing it increases the rate until another factor limits.

questions.q: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
questions.why: ADH inserts aquaporins, making urine more concentrated.

questions.q: Homeostasis mainly works by…
questions.why: A change triggers a response that reverses it.

questions.q: Guard cells open stomata by…
o: taking in K⁺, lowering water potential, then water enters and they swell
questions.why: Turgid guard cells bend apart because of uneven wall thickness.

questions.q: What causes the depolarisation in an action potential?
o: Na⁺ rushing in through voltage-gated channels
questions.why: Repolarisation then follows as K⁺ leaves.

questions.q: Myelination speeds up conduction by…
o: saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier
questions.why: Action potentials jump from node to node.

questions.q: Which plant hormone stimulates stomatal closure in drought?
questions.why: ABA triggers K⁺ loss from guard cells.

questions.q: Crossing over happens in…
questions.why: Non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange sections.

questions.q: A chi-squared test compares…
questions.why: It tests whether differences from the expected ratio are due to chance.

questions.q: Epistasis is…
o: one gene affecting the expression of another gene
questions.why: It changes expected dihybrid ratios.

questions.q: The Hardy–Weinberg equation is p² + 2pq + q² = 1. What is 2pq?
questions.why: p² = AA, 2pq = Aa, q² = aa.

questions.q: Genetic drift has the largest effect in…
questions.why: Chance changes in allele frequency matter more when numbers are small.

questions.q: Simpson's index of diversity is higher when…
o: there are many species with similar numbers
questions.why: Diversity includes both richness and evenness.

questions.q: Which are the three domains?
questions.why: Domains are the highest rank in classification.

questions.q: What does PCR do?
o: Makes many copies of a DNA sequence
questions.why: Cycles of denaturing, annealing primers and extending with Taq polymerase.

questions.q: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by…
questions.why: Negatively charged DNA moves towards the anode; small fragments travel faster.
